name: Presentations
title: AI prompts for presentations and slides
description: Prompt templates to plan presentations with AI: slide outlines, turning a report into a deck, speaker notes, tough questions and choosing the right chart.
intro: The fastest route to a good deck is letting AI help with structure, not with facts. These templates start from your audience and your one message, and keep every number tied to your source.

templates.title: Slide outline from one message
templates.useWhen: You have a talk to give and a blank deck.
templates.prompt:
I am presenting to [AUDIENCE] for [MINUTES] minutes. The one thing they must remember: [ONE-SENTENCE MESSAGE]. What I want them to do afterwards: [ACTION].
Create a slide-by-slide outline (at most [N] slides): each slide title as a full sentence stating its point, 2–3 supporting bullets, and what evidence or visual belongs on it. Mark any slide where I need to supply data with [DATA NEEDED].
templates.why: Sentence titles force every slide to make a point. The [DATA NEEDED] markers stop the model inventing figures to fill the slides.

templates.title: Turn a report into slides
templates.useWhen: The analysis exists; the deck doesn't.
templates.prompt:
Turn the report between <<< and >>> into a [N]-slide deck for [AUDIENCE].
Rules: every number on a slide must appear in the report — quote it exactly and note the section it came from; the first slide is the conclusion, not an agenda; put detail in the speaker notes, not on the slides (max 25 words per slide).

Report: <<<[PASTE]>>>
templates.why: Conclusion-first respects busy audiences, and the source note makes every figure traceable when someone asks “where is that from?”.

templates.title: Speaker notes that sound natural
templates.useWhen: You know your slides but not what to say.
templates.prompt:
Write speaker notes for these slides: <<<[PASTE SLIDE TITLES AND BULLETS]>>>
Rules: conversational, as I would say it out loud; about [SECONDS] seconds per slide; include one transition sentence into the next slide; don't read the bullets word for word — explain them.
templates.why: Notes that repeat the slide make you read your slides aloud. Timing and transitions make the talk flow.

templates.title: Prepare for tough questions
templates.useWhen: The audience is senior, sceptical or both.
templates.prompt:
Here is my presentation outline: <<<[PASTE]>>>
Audience: [AUDIENCE — their priorities and likely objections].
List the 8 hardest questions they could ask, ranked by likelihood. For each, a two-sentence answer outline based only on my material, or “needs data” if my material cannot answer it.
templates.why: Rehearsing the uncomfortable questions is where AI saves the most time, and “needs data” shows exactly what to prepare.

templates.title: Simplify a crowded slide
templates.useWhen: A slide has become a wall of text.
templates.prompt:
This slide is too dense: <<<[PASTE SLIDE TEXT]>>>
Give me: a sentence-style title with the main point; at most 3 bullets of at most 8 words each; one visual (chart type or image) that could replace text; and what to move into the speaker notes.
templates.why: Hard limits force prioritisation — the model proposes what is secondary and you approve it.

templates.title: Choose the right chart
templates.useWhen: You have data and a point to prove.
templates.prompt:
I want to show: [WHAT THE DATA SHOULD PROVE]. Data: [COLUMNS AND A FEW EXAMPLE ROWS].
Recommend the chart type, what goes on each axis, what to highlight, and a title that states the takeaway. Also say which chart types would mislead with this data and why.
templates.why: The message should choose the chart, not habit. Asking what would mislead catches truncated axes and 3D pies early.
